items.title: 11.1.3 Domains and Ranges of Cosecant Function

blocks.alt: Unit circle with centre O at the origin, axes X prime X and Y prime Y. It meets the axes at A(1, 0), B(0, 1), C(minus 1, 0) and D(0, minus 1). The terminal side OP, drawn as an arrow, makes angle theta with OX; P(x, y) is on the circle, M is the foot of the perpendicular PM on OX, OM = x and MP = y.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.1 (repeated from 11.1): unit circle with P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
\[\csc\theta = \frac{1}{y},\quad y \ne 0\]
\(\Rightarrow\) terminal side \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) should not coincide with \(OX\) or \(OX'\) (the \(X\)-axis)
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne 0, \pm\pi, \pm 2\pi, \ldots\]
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne n\pi,\ \text{where } n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Domain of cosecant function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid x = n\pi,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine: \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\). Its denominator \(y\) is the same as that of cotangent (\(\cot\theta = \frac{x}{y}\)), so cosecant and cotangent have the same domain: every angle except those whose terminal side lies on the \(X\)-axis.

As \(\csc\theta\) attains all values except those between \(-1\) and \(1\),
Range of cosecant function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid -1 < x < 1\}\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The reason is the same as for secant, now with \(y\): for \(0 < y \le 1\) we get \(\frac{1}{y} \ge 1\), and for \(-1 \le y < 0\) we get \(\frac{1}{y} \le -1\).
So \(\csc\theta \ge 1\) or \(\csc\theta \le -1\), i.e. the range is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). The end values occur at \(\csc\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\) and \(\csc\frac{3\pi}{2} = -1\).
The following table summarizes the domains and ranges of the trigonometric functions:

blocks.caption: Domains and ranges of the trigonometric functions (the book's summary table)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The table is easy to remember in three pairs:
1. \(\sin\) and \(\cos\): no denominator, so domain \(\mathbb{R}\); range \([-1, 1]\).
2. \(\tan\) and \(\sec\): denominator \(\cos x\), so remove \((2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\) where \(\cos x = 0\).
3. \(\cot\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}\): denominator \(\sin x\), so remove \(n\pi\) where \(\sin x = 0\).
For the ranges: \(\tan\) and \(\cot\) take every real value; \(\sec\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}\) take every value except those strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\).
(\(\csc\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}\) are two names of the same function; the book uses both.)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: A frequent short question: "Find the domain and range of \(y = \operatorname{cosec} x\)." Write both parts in full: domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\), range \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). Writing only one of them loses marks.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{y}\) needs \(y \ne 0\): domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\), the same as cotangent.
2. Range of cosecant: \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), the same as secant.
3. The summary table: sin, cos (all \(\mathbb{R}\); \([-1, 1]\)), tan, sec (exclude \((2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\)), cot, cosec (exclude \(n\pi\)).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Giving cosecant the domain of secant. Cosecant fails where \(\sin\theta = 0\) (\(n\pi\)), secant where \(\cos\theta = 0\) (\((2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\)).
2. Writing the range of cosecant as \(\mathbb{R} - [-1, 1]\). That would remove \(\pm 1\) too, but \(\operatorname{cosec}\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\). Only the open interval \((-1, 1)\) is removed.
